speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will speak on the first area and my colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu, will cover the second.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling will then touch on support for families undergoing divorce from the MSF perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Family disputes are not like other kinds of disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They often involve a lot of emotions, psychological wounds and vulnerable parties, particularly children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You contrast that with the usual litigation process which generally pits the parties as adversaries and looks to the past to determine who was right and wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The changes we have made over the years reflect this approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may also access the handout through the SG Parl MP mobile app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will explain, one, the need for change; two, the key changes that we are proposing; and three, what we hope to achieve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the years, we have progressively refined the maintenance enforcement framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This includes introducing new sanctions against maintenance defaulters, such as mandatory financial counselling, community service orders and credit bureau reporting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nevertheless, we still see a fairly high number of cases of non-compliance with maintenance orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And 15% to 20% of these were repeat applications made within the same year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some applicants made three to four applications to enforce the same maintenance order within a year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you see these numbers, you can understand that behind these numbers, there are also anxiety, frustration, other real-life consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Especially for the applicants – they are usually women, struggling with supporting the children, their jobs, while not getting any maintenance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members have given voice to these concerns before.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They include Ms Jessica Tan, Dr Tan Wu Meng and others who spoke about this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Single parents struggling with job stress, caregiving, other responsibilities and they need to take time off work to attend enforcement hearings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some bring their children to the Court hearings because they do not have alternate care arrangements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At this point, I think it is useful for me to share the facts relating to two cases, as illustrations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first, I will refer to one of the parties as Mdm A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Following her divorce, she had care and control of the parties’ two young children; her ex-husband was ordered to pay child maintenance at $1,500 a month.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two years after the divorce, Mdm A had not received any maintenance payments, though she had taken out enforcement proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She was left to support her two children and elderly parents alone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is how she described her frustrations in an email that she sent to me, and I quote: “Monies have to be spent each   an individual seeks legal advice; monies that most ex-spouses can ill-afford.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Perhaps this is why most give up the fight, because they can no longer afford to pay for another Court hearing and receive another ruling that will not be enforced.” The second case, I will call the lady Mdm B.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Like Mdm A, Mdm B also had care and control of the parties’ two young children, and her ex-husband was ordered to maintain her and the children at $1,500 per month.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But for five years, from 2017 to 2022, Mdm B did not receive any payments from her ex-husband, save for a one-time payment of $50, even after she had filed multiple enforcement applications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For his breaches, the ex-husband was sentenced to prison, one to two days each time, but he still did not pay, despite having the means to pay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She coped single-handedly to support her children through primary school and borrowed from friends and neighbours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I have just described for Mdm A and Mdm B is the unfortunate reality for some.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It arises because some husbands just refuse to pay and I am referring to those who can pay but would not pay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is quite separate if they just cannot pay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the issues, first, there are limited means of obtaining information on the parties’ assets and means.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This makes it difficult to distinguish between respondents who cannot pay maintenance and those who simply refuse to pay because the information is not fully in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this then often leads to a second problem, which is repeat non-compliance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For respondents who refuse to pay, the Court may find it difficult to make more targeted enforcement orders because it does not have the full information on their assets and means.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the Court processes provide for applications and getting this information, actually getting it into Court can be a challenge at times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And for respondents who cannot pay, they just do not have the money and the Courts keep making the orders, they will simply continue to miss maintenance payments, without some other form of intervention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, the process can be time-consuming, resource-intensive and difficult to navigate, especially for self-represented parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, under this Bill, what are we trying to do?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are creating a new Maintenance Enforcement Process – I will call it MEP – to address these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The MEP will seek to strengthen deterrence against respondents who refuse to pay; and it will try and facilitate more sustainable outcomes for respondents who genuinely cannot pay and it will try and increase access to justice for applicants, especially those who are self-represented.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A key part of the proposals is the establishment of a new unit of Maintenance Enforcement Officers (MEOs).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may also access the handout through the SG Parl MP mobile app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An application to enforce a maintenance order can be made online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At this stage, the applicant can also directly apply online for financial assistance, allowing such help to be given as early in the process as possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After this, the parties must submit documents on their financial circumstances to the MEO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a major step and a game changer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This power will be subject to safeguards, including restrictions on the use of information obtained by MEOs and, in some cases, requiring MEOs to obtain a Court order when seeking information from third parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the MEO’s fact-finding powers, the MEOs and the Court will be better able to distinguish between respondents who cannot pay and those who refuse to pay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the former, the MEOs will be able to refer them to Social Service Offices for financial assistance and other support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the fact-finding is completed, the parties will have to attend conciliation sessions with the MEO, who can recommend solutions and facilitate settlement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The MEO will report to the Court on the parties' financial circumstances and the conciliation sessions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will relieve the party asking for maintenance – the wife – from having to take on the burden of getting the facts, spending a lot of money on legal fees and, hopefully, it will also reduce the amount of effort a wife has to put in to get maintenance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court will take into account the MEO's report when deciding on the application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court can vary any maintenance order, taking into account the financial position of the parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where the parties have not settled and the Court orders the respondent to pay maintenance, the Court must make what is known as a Show-Payment Order (SPO).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When making the SPO, the Court must generally also specify a term of imprisonment that the respondent may be liable for if the respondent breaches the SPO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This continued monitoring, coupled with strong deterrence, should reduce repeated defaults in at least a fair number of cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the information provided by the MEO, the Court will also be better able to make more targeted and effective enforcement orders to recover arrears – for example, an order for attachment of a debt – and can do so without the applicant having to apply separately, or specifically, for such orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the post-hearing stage, the MEP caters for several possible scenarios of default.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will not cover these scenarios and the consequences of default specifically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The details are in the infographic that has been handed out and, of course, in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Members will see that, in general, the consequences for failing to show proof of payment, in accordance with the SPO, are immediate and serious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a respondent defaults on the SPO with no good cause shown, he may be sentenced to imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The MEP also provides a more streamlined process for enforcing maintenance payments, where a respondent defaults on such payments shortly after an SPO expires.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is one further area of change to the maintenance enforcement process, which is not shown in the infographic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under the existing law, an applicant who suspects that a respondent intends to dissipate, or has dissipated assets to frustrate the maintenance claim, can apply for an injunction or a clawback order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, the applicant will likely face evidential difficulties in proving the respondent's intent to dissipate property specifically to frustrate a maintenance order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To address this, we will create a rebuttable presumption of the respondent's intent to dissipate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under the proposed changes, this presumption will be raised if the applicant can show an impending or relevant dissipation, depending on whether an injunction or clawback order is sought and that the impending or relevant dissipation, as the case may be, will or did frustrate the enforcement of the maintenance order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With these changes, the burden is on the respondent to prove that he did not intend to frustrate the maintenance claim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will, hopefully, deter parties from circumventing maintenance orders through the wilful dissipation of assets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do we hope to achieve with these changes?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Overall, these changes will improve access to justice, especially for self-represented parties, who, as I said earlier, are involved in the vast majority of maintenance enforcement cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Members can empathise, it is difficult to expect parties to move on when maintenance obligations are breached, especially if the breaches occur repeatedly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such breaches can also spur retaliatory action by the other side and pull both parties further apart.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I conclude, Sir, I would like to thank the FJC judges, Court staff, the Family Bar, academics, our social service partner agencies and other stakeholders for working with us on these reforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We hope to continue to work with all of these partners to shape our family justice system to achieve more positive outcomes in protecting, restoring and healing families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This Bill represents another step forward in this journey.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Minister Shanmugam has touched upon one key area of reform in the Bill – the new Maintenance Enforcement Process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will now turn to the other key area of reform this Bill seeks to effect – the enhancement of Court proceedings and procedure in the Family Justice Courts (FJC).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The changes we are making in this area support the ideals outlined earlier in Minister Shanmugam's speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some of the reforms under this area arise out of the recommendations of the Committee to Review and Enhance Reforms in the Family Justice System, or the RERF Committee for short.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The RERF Committee, which consisted of representatives from MSF, MinLaw and FJC, was formed in 2017 and released its recommendations in September 2019.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Its recommendations were aimed at, amongst others, further strengthening the Therapeutic Justice elements in the family justice system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government then consulted the public and stakeholders on the RERF Committee's recommendations and has since then been working to implement the recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, MSF announced in 2022 that the Mandatory Co-Parenting Programme will be extended from only parents who disagree on divorce and ancillary matters, to all parents with minor children on the Simplified Track.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will help more parents to focus on making informed decisions that prioritise the well-being of their children in the divorce process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This Bill implements the remaining recommendations of the RERF Committee that require legislative changes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will now turn to the key reforms in this Bill which enhance proceedings and procedure in the FJC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The amendments which I will be speaking about can be grouped into four buckets: one, promoting efficiency in Court proceedings; two, enhancing and clarifying the judge-led approach; three, simplifying Court terminology; and four, other miscellaneous and technical amendments to clarify, enhance and streamline FJC processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In its report, the RERF Committee observed that the filing of unnecessary applications in family proceedings prolongs proceedings, promotes acrimony and strains judicial resources.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is a particularly pertinent issue in family proceedings, which are emotionally charged.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Such strong emotions can hinder rational thinking and cloud judgement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are cases where parties who are caught up in the heat of the litigation resort to taking out unnecessary and unmeritorious applications in Court to vex the other party or to paint the other party in a bad light.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, one party may make repeated applications against the other party for discovery of documents which have little relevance or evidential value to the issue at hand.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Not only are such applications a waste of the parties' time and the Court's resources, but such conduct can harm the relationship of the parties and their family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The RERF Committee acknowledged that not every case involving the filing of multiple applications is necessarily an abuse of process, and, in any event, the ability to strike out or dismiss an application on the ground of abuse of process should be exercised with caution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To ensure that unmeritorious applications which detract from important issues are weeded out at an early stage, the Committee recommended that, in appropriate circumstances, the permission of the Court must be sought before a further application can be filed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The new section 11A of the Family Justice Act will implement the Committee's recommendation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are two parts to the new section 11A.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The first part of section 11A deals with certain applications by a party in relation to an order already made in previous proceedings, for example, an application to vary, suspend or set aside a previous order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For ease of explaining the first part of section 11A, I shall call an application which falls into this category a "variation application".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The second part of section 11A deals with applications in proceedings which are pending before FJC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I shall call an application which falls into this category an "interlocutory application".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Section 11A will promote a more efficient resolution of family proceedings and also reduce the acrimony and stresses which may be inflicted on the parties' relationship through the filing of unnecessary applications and documents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As the mother exhibited physical and emotionally abusive behaviour, the Court granted protection orders against the mother after the divorce, in favour of the father and the two children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: After the protection orders were granted, over a period of three years, the mother filed close to 15 applications in Court against Ms C, her father and her sibling.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This includes more than five applications to revoke the protection orders granted in favour of Ms C, her father and her sibling.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In the case of the protection order obtained by Ms C, the mother's applications to revoke the protection order were dismissed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms C conveyed that each of the applications filed has taken a huge emotional toll on her family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With each application filed by her mother, they ended up having to take time off work to spend time on Court proceedings and be subject to the mental stress of facing the mother for an extended period of time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With greater judicial control over the filing of unnecessary applications, we hope that circumstances where parties like Ms C and her family live in fear of having to be dragged back into proceedings by estranged family members involuntarily will be reduced.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Instead, families will be given the space to heal and move on, without having to return to Court repeatedly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The new powers in section 11A will also help to enhance the efficiency of family proceedings by giving FJC the powers to weed out unmeritorious applications which unnecessarily protract proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Minister Shanmugam had earlier explained that the judge-led approach was introduced in 2014 to allow FJC to proactively manage the manner in which cases are run in family proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The RERF Committee had recommended that there be greater clarity and guidance to family judges on how the judge-led approach is to be applied.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This Bill will, therefore, clarify and strengthen the judge-led approach through three key provisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, providing that judges may make orders of a substantive nature on their own motion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, empowering judges to impose restrictions on cross-examination in circumstances prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Third, providing that the Family Justice Rules (FJR) may set out the modes by which a child's wishes may be determined by the Court and this may include judicial interviews.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For the first key provision, the RERF Committee recommended that the Court be expressly empowered to make substantive orders on its own motion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Family proceedings often involve litigants-in-person or self-represented parties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They may not be aware of the variety of orders or directions available, or which ones are needed to address their particular issues, or which may be made to safeguard the interests and well-being of their children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In such situations, the new section 11B allows the Court to make the necessary orders to deal with the issues effectively, even if neither party has asked for the order specifically.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For instance, the Court may, in the course of conducting a case conference, make interim access orders to ensure that the child continues to have contact time with a parent until the matter can be resolved through mediation or determined in a formal hearing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court may do so even if none of the parties makes an application for an interim access order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The rules of natural justice will be preserved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court's power to make an order of a substantive nature under section 11B may only be exercised if: every person likely to be affected by the order is first given an opportunity to be heard concerning the order; and the Court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to make the order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At present, rule 101A of the FJR already allows the Court to limit the scope and duration of cross-examination, or to disallow direct cross-examination in two situations: (a) a family violence trial in proceedings under Part 7 of the Women's Charter; (b) an application under section 67(1) of the Women's Charter to vary, suspend or revoke a protection order or an expedited order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The direct cross-examination of a victim of family violence by their alleged perpetrator can expose the victim to significant re-traumatisation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Subjecting the victims to the usual cross-examination may also affect their ability to give clear and cogent evidence in support of their case.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: After what has happened between them, victims may also find it challenging to effectively cross-examine their alleged perpetrator.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: That being said, cross-examination is fundamental in testing and challenging the evidence of a witness and to accurately determine the facts on which the Court decides the matter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The RERF Committee considered the approaches in England and Australia on prohibiting cross-examination in family violence cases and recommended that the Courts should be empowered to restrict cross-examination in specified circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court's powers under the new section 11C will complement its existing powers under the Evidence Act to, among others, forbid any question which appears to the Court to be intended to insult or annoy or appears to be needlessly offensive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The intention is for the prescribed modes to expressly include interviews conducted by a judge with a child, in addition to the variety of other methods which may be used to hear a child's voice, such as through the Child Representatives or an assessment by a mental health professional.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In the context of matrimonial proceedings under the Women's Charter, section 125 of the Women's Charter provides that in deciding in whose custody a child should be placed, the paramount consideration shall be the welfare of the child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Section 125 also specifically requires the Court to have regard to: (a) the wishes of the parents; and (b) the wishes of a child where he or she is of an age to express an independent opinion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, section 125 does not provide for the modes by which the child's wishes may be determined.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The RERF Committee, in its report, discussed the benefits of judges conducting interviews with children and noted that, in Singapore, there have been cases where judges have conducted interviews with children to reach outcomes that serve the interests of the child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: An example of such a case is AZB v AZC   SGHCF 1.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In that case, the High Court Judge interviewed three children between the ages of 11 and 13 in a dispute between their parents on care and control and access arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Judge noted that there were indications that the children wished to speak with her.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The children were mature enough to express their views on matters that impacted their lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In deciding that it would be in the children's welfare to increase the access time with their mother, the Judge relied on, among other things, the Judge's conversations with the children which corroborated the finding that the children enjoyed access time with their mother.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Committee mentioned that there has been research highlighting children's wishes to be more involved in the decisions that may affect their lives profoundly and their dissatisfaction with the indirect processes that are available to them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Committee recommended, therefore, that it should be made clear that the judge-led approach allows for a judge to interview a child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It should be noted that each case is unique, with different considerations applying to each family and each child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is not in every case that a judicial interview of children is suitable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In some cases, the Court may assess that it would be more appropriate to appoint a Child Representative, who is a trained professional appointed by the Court to represent the voice of a child and present an objective assessment of care arrangements which are in the child's best interest, or other professional, to hear from the child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Moving on to the next bucket of reforms, the Bill will amend various pieces of legislation to modernise and simplify nomenclature for family proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, "Plaintiff" will be replaced by "Applicant", "Defendant" will be replaced by "Respondent" and "Writ for divorce" will be replaced by "originating application for divorce".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will be in line with the amendments made to Court terminology in civil Court proceedings under the Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Act 2021 and the Rules of Court 2021.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In the new Family Justice Rules to be introduced, the simplified terminology will also be adopted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These changes will make it easier for Court users and members of the public to understand family proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will amplify the existing efforts by the Government and Judiciary to enhance access to justice, especially for persons who cannot afford legal representation, by simplifying Court processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The last bucket of reforms relates to various miscellaneous and technical amendments to clarify, enhance and streamline processes in the FJC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will elaborate on two of these amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, on mediation and other alternative dispute resolution processes or "ADR processes" for short.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Currently, the Family Justice Act provides that a Family Court or Youth Court, respectively, may, on its own motion or upon the application of any party, order any party or any child who is the subject of proceedings, to undergo mediation or counselling, or to participate in any family support programme or activity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court also has powers to order a party or child to undergo other ADR processes, or to attend professional clinical or therapeutic intervention sessions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Amendments will also be made to provide that a Family Court or Youth Court may make the appropriate and necessary orders where a person fails to comply with the Court's orders to attend mediation or other ADR process, such as an order staying proceedings until the orders are complied with.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The amendments will align the position under the Family Justice Act with that in section 43 of the State Courts Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Depending on the circumstances of the case, in certain situations, instead of incurring time and costs in enforcement or bankruptcy proceedings, it may be more sensible and in the interests of both parties, for the Court to grant a short reprieve to the judgment debtor, or to allow the judgment debtor to pay the judgment creditor by way of instalments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is especially important in family proceedings where further litigation would put an additional strain on the fractured relationship and adversely impact children involved in the proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will not go into details on all the other amendments under the Bill, but Members are free to raise any questions that they may have on those amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To conclude, I would like to express our gratitude to the members of the RERF Committee for their recommendations, and the stakeholders and members of the public who have taken the time to give us feedback on the family justice system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With your feedback and suggestions, we were better able to shape the reforms in this Bill to resolve the real issues faced by families and children in family proceedings and to better protect, restore and heal families and children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Time will be required and work will need to be put in to operationalise some of the changes in this Bill, including the Maintenance Enforcement Process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We hope you will continue to give us support and feedback, to operationalise the reforms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Minister Shanmugam and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu have explained the objective and details of the Bill in their speeches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At MSF, our aim is to nurture strong families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: That is why we had designated the year 2022 as the Year of Celebrating SG Families and launched "A Singapore Made for Families 2025", a national plan to strengthen and support families through all life stages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The foundation for strong families is laid even before marriage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When a couple contemplates marrying and starting their own family, support is provided through the Marriage Preparation Programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As they embark on this new phase of life, they can seek mentoring support from Licensed Solemnisers and community volunteers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This foundation is continually built on during their marriage, through access to marriage and parenting support programmes organised by Families for Life, or FFL in short.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will be stepping up outreach at the local level via FFL@Community which will be expanded to all towns by 2025.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When friction arises, families can seek help from the Strengthening Families Programme@Family Service Centres, or FAM@FSCs in short.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The 10 FAM@FSC Centres island-wide provide counselling services, such as for marital strains or conflict among family members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our hope is for families to be able to successfully work through and come through adversity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, we recognise that some families may come to the point where they begin to contemplate divorce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our aim is to save the marriage and, apart from family counselling, the Family Assist Portal provides couples with the relevant resources to make an informed decision regarding their marriage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Where divorce is truly inevitable, we seek to foster Therapeutic Justice in the divorce process to bring about healing so that the family can move on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I had led focus group discussions and engaged over 120 divorcees in 2020 and 2021 to understand the divorce process and the difficult decisions they had to make.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Arising from those discussions and the intent to foster Therapeutic Justice, we have introduced several initiatives in recent years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In January 2022, the Women's Charter (Amendment) Bill was passed in this House.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To encourage parents to make informed decisions regarding their divorce that prioritise the well-being of their children, we had made it mandatory for all divorcing parents with minor children to go through a Co-Parenting Programme, or CPP in short.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We had also sought to reduce acrimony in the divorce process and introduced the Divorce by Mutual Agreement (DMA) of the Irretrievable Breakdown of the Marriage as a sixth fact that parties may cite to show that their marriage has irretrievably broken down.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The changes to CPP and the introduction of DMA will be brought into force in 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To ensure that children impacted by divorce are supported in navigating this difficult period, we have empowered the Court to advise that minor children attend the Programme for Children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, we have heard the pain of parents who were unable to obtain access to their children as ordered by the Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We had amended the Women's Charter to introduce a new suite of measures for the enforcement of child access.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are working with FJC on further simplifying the enforcement process so that there is no need to seek leave of Court before an application is made for enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is within this wider landscape of support for the family that the proposed MEP will come in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The MEP will facilitate more sustainable maintenance outcomes for parties, allowing parents to both do their part in co-parenting their children and move on from the divorce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For respondents who genuinely cannot pay, as well as for applicants who face day-to-day difficulties due to non-payment of maintenance, MSF will now be able to provide financial assistance in a more timely manner, where appropriate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The current maintenance enforcement process, from the perspective of the applicant, can be time- and resource-intensive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For the low-income, this can result in great inconvenience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For low-wage mothers, who already face the stress of caring for their children, having to return to Court to enforce their maintenance order could be the final straw that breaks them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, the assets of divorcees and their financial situation are often not transparent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This makes it difficult for the judge to determine if the respondent truly cannot afford to pay maintenance, or if the respondent can afford to pay maintenance but is unwilling to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The new process will simplify the process, reduce the number of trips the applicant has to make to Court and reduce the duration of the current maintenance enforcement process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, after obtaining information on the respondent’s financial situation, the MEO will be empowered to make recommendations for parties to reach a reasonable out-of-Court settlement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Third, the MEO has the power to report the information to the Court, which will support the Court to make maintenance enforcement orders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, previously, should the respondent have attempted to frustrate the maintenance order by dissipating their assets, although the applicant may suspect that the respondent had such an intention, it can be very difficult to prove.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The MEP complements earlier efforts by MSF to strengthen therapeutic justice in the divorce process, through the 2022 Women’s Charter (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in conceptualising the many enhancements to divorce support, including the MEP, MSF and MinLaw have met and spoken with many groups of stakeholders, including parents who have gone through divorces, law practitioners and social service agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is clear that we all share the same vision for our families, families that endeavour to put the needs of their family members, their children first, even as they navigate difficult circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is our hope that parents will prioritise the welfare of their children and work together to cooperatively co-parent their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I will touch on just two aspects of the Bill and I will deal with them in turn.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first aspect is the desire for Family Court proceedings to be simpler and to produce fair outcomes without undue delay.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One way of doing this is by providing Judges a greater ambit to decide on key matters that protect public interest, as well as the interests of vulnerable parties, such as children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary Ms Rahayu Mahzam took pains to outline the workings of this provision in her speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As she mentioned, this proposal emanated from a recommendation of the Committee to Review and Enhance Reforms in the Family Justice System, or the RERF Committee, in 2019.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the report, the RERF Committee explained that a judge-led approach will have, amongst others, the salutary effect of reducing acrimony between parties and avoiding protracted proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I agree with the rationale outlined by the REFF Committee.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from strengthening the Therapeutic Justice element in the family proceedings, reposing such a power with the Court, in my respectful view, may also serve to guard against situations where the husband and wife together agree to post-divorce arrangements that may not be suitable for the children of the marriage, particularly young children who are of school-going age.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such situations, unfortunately, occur from time to time despite the common wisdom that they should be prioritising the needs of their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I made this point during the Ministry of National Development (MND) Committee of Supply (COS) debate earlier this year when I spoke on the topic of inclusive public housing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister highlighted in his speech that family disputes are unique because, amongst others, they involve vulnerable children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The interests of vulnerable children may not necessarily be aligned with those of their parents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: During the debate, I mentioned that I have come across cases where the husband and wife, for reasons of expediency, decided on arrangements, such as selling their HDB flat early, without having the prospect of securing proper housing arrangements or even considering schooling arrangements for the young children of the marriage.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In these cases, as there was agreement between the parties, the Court proceeded to endorse the parties' agreement on the assumption that the parents have catered for the needs of their young children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is only after disposing the matrimonial property that the issue of the children's interest not being sufficiently safeguarded came to the fore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such cases, the parent who has custody of the children may then make an appeal to HDB for urgent accommodation, presenting HDB with a fait accompli.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we all know, such requests are not easily acceded to.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, the children suffer from the decisions of their parents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even without the involvement of young children, I have seen situations where, post-divorce, one party to the proceedings would apply to HDB for urgent public housing on the basis that the Court had ordered the sale of the matrimonial property, leaving that person without a roof over his or her head.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me that part of the problem lies with the fact that there exists an information asymmetry between the parties to the divorce proceedings, HDB and the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: HDB would be in the dark about what the parties represented to the Court about housing arrangements post-divorce.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Court may not know whether the parties' proposed housing arrangement is feasible as HDB's criteria are not cast in stone and it does exercise discretion on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second aspect of the Bill that I intend to speak on deals with proposals aimed at facilitating better maintenance outcomes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister in his speech spoke about real life cases involving husbands who could pay but just obstinately refused to pay, forcing the single mothers to bear heavy responsibilities of bringing up their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, they simply did not have the bandwidth to pursue their ex-husbands to pay maintenance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And these defaulting spouses may even get away with their offending behaviour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Speaker of Parliament, in his capacity as the Minister for Social and Family Development in 2017, in a Family Justice Forum, said as follows: "… aintenance issues continue to be an area of concern for some parties, even after the divorce has been finalised.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the parent who requires financial contributions from the other towards the child's upkeep, having to return to Court to enforce a maintenance order can be tedious and frustrating.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially so when the other parent has the means to pay but refuses to do so." The hon Minister, in his speech, pointed out that in the 2022 White Paper on Singapore Women's Development, maintenance enforcement reform was advocated as a priority area.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is precisely the problem that the introduction of the Maintenance Enforcement Officers (MEOs), who will have the powers to obtain more accurate information about the respondents' financial circumstances, is intended to address and I support this move.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With this, the MEO will be able to ascertain whether the respondent does not have the capacity to pay or he has the capacity but refuses to pay.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through this, we can have quicker enforcement action against the recalcitrant respondents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will, in turn, put similarly minded persons, who may think that they could get away with not complying with maintenance Court orders, on notice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question I have is, why is it proposed that the MEO be an officer appointed by the Executive Branch of the Government instead of the Judiciary?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, under Rule 114B of the Family Justice Rules 2014, the Court has the power to appoint a public officer as a Maintenance Record Officer, the MRO, who is considered as an officer of the Family Justice Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The MRO has quasi-judicial powers similar to what is being proposed for the MEO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This includes the power to interview parties to the proceedings; and obtain documents and information on the financial circumstances of a party to proceedings from the party directly or from any other person, with the consent of the party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, the MRO may be required to prepare for the Court a written report setting out his opinion on the financial circumstances of the party and whether he is able to pay maintenance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This report may be relied on by the Court as evidence of the matters stated in the report.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also mirrors what the MEO is supposed to do under the proposed maintenance regime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the MEO is supposed to take over the tasks of the MRO, may I ask why it is proposed that the MEO be an officer of the Executive arm of the Government instead of the Judiciary?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we all know, our Constitution is based on the separation of powers doctrine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are three pillars of Government; the judiciary is an independent pillar of the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister may make regulations prescribing fees payable to an MEO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, it is expressly proposed that the MEO ascertain the facts and circumstances of the case, assist the Court and issue a report that the Court can take cognisance of.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: An MRO, on the other hand, is an officer of the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, there is less of an issue for an officer of the Court assisting the Court on the same matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How would public interest be better served by siting this responsibility with the Executive rather than the Judiciary?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to clarify that I support the MEO proposal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am merely pointing out that, as there is an important shift of responsibility from the Judiciary to the Executive that is being proposed, it is incumbent for the Executive arm of the Government to explain the reason for assuming this responsibility clearly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the ambit of the power to be reposed on MEO with respect to information gathering.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister mentioned in his speech about the problem posed by respondents dissipating their assets to third parties and that would frustrate the applicant's endeavour to get paid under maintenance orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is one big area of concern and I am glad to note that there is a proposal to reverse the evidential burden so as to alleviate the problems on the part of the applying spouses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another area where there could be a significant challenge is where the respondent has assets and properties which are held in the names of proxies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To make headway on such matters, there will be a need to conduct investigations, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These investigations will include the relationship between the respondent and an identified proxy; the personal and financial background of the proxy; and any financial transactions between the respondent and the proxy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is, therefore, important to ensure that the MEO has sufficient powers to do all these so as to be able to lift the veil of secrecy between the respondent and his proxy, depending on the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, I note that an MEO may avail himself of information from banks and prescribed third parties which I understand refers to specific Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Does it refer to any other Government agency that is not prescribed?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or does it only refer to any private person, and this may include legal entities, who may have relevant information?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In summary, my first point on the leadership of judges in this process, as well as a whole-of-Government lens in information sharing, speaks to an important point on efficient implementation of justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The ties that bind us, husband to wife, are ties that can be severed by divorce proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the tie that binds a citizen to his fellow men, and to his country, remains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I support the intent of this Bill to improve the enforcement process for maintenance payments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many spouses actually even gave up trying to get their payments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under the current system, a common and frustrating experience for many is that former spouses delay or refuse to pay their maintenance for their ex-partners or children and do not pay up until their former partners take up an application in Court to enforce maintenance payments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Frequently, for those who can afford to pay, the payment can even be at the doorstep of the Court room, just before the hearing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On such an occasion, I understand that the applicant does not even get its legal costs paid despite having to take out such application and engaging a lawyer in the process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And for many who default on their maintenance payments, their former spouses often had to take multiple applications.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many applicants had to take leave from work each time and would even lose income from spending time instructing their lawyers and attending Court hearings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many, I am told, just gave up after a few tries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They just could not afford the time and efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is important; it will help to deter and weed out those who game the system by refusing to pay until at least an application for enforcement is made.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the said clause allows the MEO to provide an interim report to any party whom the MEO thinks any information in the MEO’s report ought to be brought to the attention of such a party, the Bill does not seem to require the MEO to provide the full report to the applicant, the respondent or both.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is somewhat unusual in our civil legal processes as documents or evidence to be considered in any proceedings are traditionally required to be disclosed to all parties in the same proceedings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, it would also be fair to both parties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, the applicant should know why the application fails and both parties should know its contents to decide whether it is fair and should be appealed against.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If the respondent can afford his maintenance payments, disclosure of such report to the applicant may also deter the respondent from trying to hide his financial status.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also note that clause 90 allows for redaction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask what type of information will likely be redacted from this report or excluded from the interim report if the judge decides that such report should be given to either party.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that the new MEP will significantly reduce incidents of deliberate and late or non-payment of maintenance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While divorce is never easy, it can be especially challenging for women who often find themselves struggling to manage their livelihoods while ensuring the well-being of their charges, especially children in their custody or part custody.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When women, especially mothers, go through a divorce, they are often left to manage the household and take care of the children on their own.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They need financial stability and independence to rebuild their lives after a divorce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, for many women, this is easier said than done, especially if their spouses were the sole-breadwinners in their households.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These women are often sandwiched, caring for their young children, elderly parents and households, and they find it challenging to balance their caregiving responsibilities with the need to provide for their families financially.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The situation becomes even more complicated for women who are going through a divorce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The circumstances in these women’s lives have not changed, the young are still young, the elderly, elderly, and the infirmed, infirmed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The only thing that has changed is the added complexity of livelihoods and financial stability that our women now have to take care of.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It could be a classic case of out of the frying pan into the fire for many women caught in these double binds.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my work in my constituency and in NTUC’s Women and Family Unit, I often meet women in such double binds, seeking help and support, sometimes with their young children, often in tears and at a loss of what to do, with no jobs, no CPF and no savings.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many a time, their ex-husbands have gone missing and with that, too, all hopes and promise of any maintenance orders due to these women through their divorce settlements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I sometimes also meet women, who hide their shame of being stuck in an abusive marriage, unable to move on, as they are financially unable to care for themselves and their children and are afraid, if they do indeed get divorced, that their ex-husbands will not fulfil their maintenance orders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I met Emily – not her real name – many times over the past two years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Initially, Emily’s issues pertained to financial assistance she needed for her four children, the oldest who is just 14 years old when I met them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we got to know each other better over the months, Emily shared that she had a rocky and high tension marriage with her husband and had thought long and seriously about leaving the marriage.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, she continued being a dutiful wife, taking care of the household, their four children and her in-laws who are both staying with her.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She has a part-time job, earning less than $2,000, and this is barely enough to cover her household of eight.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Earlier this year, Emily reached out once again, distraught that her husband had gone missing in action (MIA) and his last known location was in Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He had abandoned the family, leaving her to take care of the family, the flat mortgage and even his business debts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Emily is seeking a divorce, but is worried that her husband would not pay maintenance and, should the divorce be granted, that she would be forced to sell her marital home, leaving her and her family with no roof over their heads.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am pleased to note from Minister Shanmugam that the process is now online in the new enforcement process.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must work towards creating a family justice system that is not just fair but enabling for all.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NTUC's Women and Family Unit is committed to supporting women, including single mothers and divorcees, to return to work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We believe that empowering and enabling women to be financially independent is a very important part of the support network needed, especially after a divorce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This combines a six-week paid flexible training programme with a transition into a flexible work arrangement (FWA) with good salaries and clear career pathways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is essential that, as a community, we create the right conditions for women to transit into the workforce smoothly and help to retain them in the workforce by recognising the need to balance livelihoods with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the larger context of family justice, I call upon our Singaporean community – social and business – to come together to enable our sisters to be financially independent, above and beyond the protections of the improvements to this reform Bill.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Companies must redesign their jobs such that FWAs become a business and social norm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Family Courts can consider, in addition to specifying clinical and therapeutic intervention sessions, also job and upskilling workshops to ensure that women have access to the resources and support they need to rebuild their lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must equip our women with the means to long-term financial stability, peace of mind in managing their caregiving responsibilities and the choice to return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am supportive of this Bill and the efforts to strengthen family Therapeutic Justice.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My speech today aims to seek clarifications on certain aspects of the Bill, particularly that relating to providing greater support for both the applicants and respondents to the maintenance enforcement process.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, I will also be speaking on related issues to improve on the education and housing needs of children involved in a divorce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This step comes after the MEO has obtained relevant information from the involved parties and determines that one or more of the parties involved would require financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate the inclusion of such a step in the Maintenance Enforcement Process.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As what my hon friend Member of Parlliament Jamus Lim alluded to in his Committee of Supply (COS) speech this year, the dignity of the needy should be retained even while applying for financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if the parties referred to a social service officer (SSO) would still need to complete the relevant paperwork and go through a similar application process for financial assistance, had he or she made the application to the SSO separately?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, under section 86, the MEO will be empowered to obtain information about the parties' assets and means from stipulated entities, such as certain Government agencies, banks and the Central Depository.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, if the MEO and the Courts already have access to such information, should we do away with the requirement for parties to the maintenance enforcement process to submit documents, such as bank statements, which is detailed in the MEP process workflow?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such a move would greatly reduce the administrative burden of applicants especially, and reduce the emotional burden faced by the parties involved as they navigate through this patch of troubled waters in their lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the MEP workflow allows for the smooth application of financial assistance, it does not guarantee that each application will yield a successful outcome.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Section 81 allows for the Court to "vary, suspend, discharge, rescind, set aside or revoke the maintenance order." This could either be due to an application by either party or a settlement by both parties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This step comes after the MEO has referred the relevant parties for financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What then happens if the application of financial assistance for the relevant parties is unsuccessful?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Potentially, such a problem would especially impact those whose income exceeds the income threshold for financial assistance but are burdened with a multitude of financial commitments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Maintenance payments are key for applicants to pay for their living expenses, foot medical bills and repay other arrears and mortgages that they have.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, with a reduction or variation in the maintenance order, divorcees would face an additional financial burden and a lower quality of life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would help to ensure that there would be minimal impact on the welfare of the parties involved, increase the efficiency of the MEP and produce sustainable maintenance outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clause 12 of the Bill states that the Family Justice Rules can prescribe the mode through which the child's wishes may be determined if the Court wishes to consider it in its ruling.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to the media release, this may include judicial interviews with the child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the case of AZB vs AZC  , the Family Justice Courts laid out that judicial interviews of children are suitable in the Singaporean context.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the ruling, Justice Debbie Ong also highlighted the difficulties faced when conducting judicial interviews of children, such as there being insufficient time available to build rapport between the judge and child, communication difficulties between the child and the judge, and discomfort towards the Court process by the child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One recommendation laid out by the Court is that judges should be equipped with the necessary skills to handle judicial interviews with the child, which could be achieved by training judicial staff.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a move seen in other countries with the common law system, such as Australia, which called for the training of judicial staff back in 1995.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, Singapore could also consider adopting a similar approach.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We could consider implementing guidelines, such as to provide an environment that facilitates the process effectively, such as determining the parties present at the meeting, the tone of the meeting and the information briefed to the child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Risks, such as parental interference, could also be mitigated by instructing parents not to ask their children about the interview.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are some of the skills and knowledge that could be imparted to judges as part of a training programme to effectively conduct a judicial interview of a child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would enable them to communicate with the child to gain a better understanding of their needs, wants and views regarding the matter, which could aid them in their judgment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Strengthening the maintenance regime is arguably a key step to ensuring that the basic living needs of children and their caregivers, such as good nutrition, are met.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, administrative procedures and issues that divorcees face could also reopen wounds and cause further trauma.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I, thus, believe there is room for us to improve on processes and policies relating to the child's education and housing needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On education, I understand that parents who have joint custody of their child need to come to a common agreement on their child's school transfer.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The relevant Court order setting out the custody arrangements pertaining to the child will be required at the point of reporting to the current school.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The parent who submits the application for the child will be required to produce a signed Letter of Consent from the other parent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To what extent is this being operationalised and practised in our schools?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The reason I am asking is also because in the MOE's step-by-step guide for primary school transfers, it is stated that, and I quote, "In making this application, I understand that should the other parents/legal guardian have any basis to contest this arrangement in the future, I will resolve this issue with him/her".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It appears that the responsibility to resolve any disputes on transfers is delegated to the parent, with no mention of any Letters of Consent or undertaking required.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When it comes to preschools, are there also similar requirements by the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) for a Letter of Consent before any enrolment or transfer is made?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Or could a parent with care and control of the child enrol him or her in a preschool, without the approval of the other parent with joint custody?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, as an individual is only allowed to be listed in one HDB flat application, the HDB requires divorced parents to come to an agreement before either party lists their child in a flat application.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Considering that we are looking at divorcees here, coming to an agreement is often easier said than done.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While one party can form a family nucleus with his or her children, the other party will not be able to.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For a young divorcee under the age of 35, for example, he or she will not be able to apply for a flat by themselves under the Singles Scheme and not be able to form a family nucleus with his or her children.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This could be especially problematic for some parents facing financial hardship or/and without family support, as it will not be practically possible for this parent to care for his or her child, without a stable place to call home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Both divorcees and their children would need a roof over their heads.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I hope our policies can recognise this and ensure that all Singaporeans can have access to housing and not have to worry about basic needs, such as access to shelter, in their divorce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, as the Chinese saying goes, "孩子是无辜的", the children are innocent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Children of divorced parents are already facing difficult circumstances and are at risk of psychological and other adjustment issues.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us continue to do all we can to better improve on the welfare of the children involved and minimise potential points of conflict in their growing up years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
