text: The Bill aims to bring about a much-needed transformation in our family justice system, focusing on the well-being of our children and families while addressing the challenges faced by parties involved in family disputes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The pain and anguish faced by families embroiled in disputes are all too familiar to all of us.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We may know of residents, friends, family members or even neighbours who have endured the emotional turmoil and financial strain that a lengthy and adversarial legal process can inflict upon families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We may know of similar scenarios where a single mother had to wait for more than a year to receive maintenance from a former spouse.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The delay in receiving maintenance payments places an immense financial burden on the single mother and her innocent children who had to suffer the consequences of this predicament.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This bold step will ensure that vulnerable parties, such as children and former spouses, receive the financial support they need in a timely manner.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Moreover, the Bill introduces the groundbreaking concept of family hearing, a major stride towards a more streamlined and effective Family Justice system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Family hearings will provide a platform for parties to discuss their disputes in a less adversarial setting and promote amicable resolutions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While the proposed Bill has many advantages, I seek clarification from the Ministry on certain aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the Bill's provisions for stronger enforcement of maintenance orders are commendable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I am concerned about the impact of the new maintenance enforcement process on low-income families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And I am concerned that these measures may be too harsh for the low-income families who are genuinely unable to pay maintenance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Also, could the Ministry elaborate on the specific measures it plans to implement to ensure compliance and deter non-compliance effectively?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How does the Ministry plan to ensure that adequate resources, such as skilled mediators and support staff, are available for the efficient functioning of these hearings?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, I am especially concerned for the more complex cases where a certified mental health practitioner may be required and, if so, would provisions be made and how would such arrangements be like?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, what measures will be put in place to address any potential power imbalances between the parties involved in these hearings?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Notwithstanding my concerns earlier, I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That will be the thrust of my speech today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This should be done by giving the Courts the discretion to order that, in appropriate cases, wives should pay maintenance to ex-husbands even if they are not incapacitated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such cases could include where the husband earns much less than his ex-wife, or is a stay-home-husband, and has borne the bulk of domestic chores and caregiving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is in contrast to the current maintenance regime in the Women’s Charter, which provides that, in a divorce, the Court may order a man to pay maintenance to his ex-wife but may order a woman to pay maintenance to her ex-husband only if he is incapacitated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I previously raised this issue in the Motion on Singapore Women’s Development in 2022.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My hon friend, Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member of Parliament Mr Gerald Giam, has also spoken on this in 2021.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, there is bipartisan support for awarding maintenance to stay-at-home dads.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hon Members Ms Carrie Tan and Mr Ang Wei Neng raised this issue in the 2022 Parliamentary debate on amendments to the Women’s Charter, and hon Members Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Louis Ng also raised this issue in the 2016 Parliamentary debate on amendments to Women’s Charter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, the number of stay-home husbands has been gradually increasing over the years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That is not an insignificant number at all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Labour Force survey for Singapore in 2022 showed that 10.6% of caregivers outside the labour force are males, whether married or unmarried.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Again, this is a not an insignificant minority.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many stay-at-home husbands, just like stay-at-home wives, have sacrificed their careers and incurred significant opportunity costs to spend years looking after their households and doing unpaid care work, such as raising the children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a result, stay-at-home husbands may have far less savings as compared to their working wives and may well be financially vulnerable in the event of a divorce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Allowing the Courts to have discretion to award maintenance to such husbands would serve to recognise their care work and unpaid contributions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would also help to safeguard the financially vulnerable spouse, whether husband or wife, which is, surely, the fundamental purpose of maintenance payments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2022, the employment rate of females aged 15 and over was 60.9%, the fourth highest in comparison with OECD developed countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With a larger proportion of women in the workforce, it could well be the case that women might out-earn men in some dual-income households and, thus, would make economic sense for the husband to take on the bulk of domestic work in a household, depending on the decisions that the husband and wife make in each particular case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, the current maintenance regime arguably reinforces traditional gendered household roles where men traditionally are regarded as “breadwinners” and women as “homemakers”, by providing that only incapacitated husbands qualify for maintenance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An Institute of Policy Studies survey of stay-at-home fathers in 2020 showed that many of the respondents, many of these stay-at-home dads, experienced “acute stigma” and family members often directed comments suggesting that they were “mooching” from their wives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, many other developed countries allow for men to claim maintenance as well, such as the United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the USA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us take a leaf from their books.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the UK government’s Guide to Spousal Maintenance, it is stated that “Spousal maintenance is a payment that’s paid by a wife or husband to their former spouse as part of their divorce.” The language used in a similar Australian government public resource is similarly gender-neutral and states: “Under the Family Law Act 1975, a person has a responsibility to financially assist their spouse, or former de facto partner, if that person cannot meet their own reasonable expenses from their personal income or assets.” In section 63 and 64 of New Zealand’s Family Proceedings Act 1980, gender-neutral language is used.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, “each spouse, civil union partner, or de facto partner is liable to maintain the other spouse, civil union partner, or de facto partner to the extent that such maintenance is necessary to meet the reasonable needs of the other spouse, civil union partner, or de facto partner, where the other spouse, civil union partner, or de facto partner cannot practicably meet the whole or any part of those needs because of any one or more of the circumstances specified in subsection (2).” So, the language is gender neutral.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To quote from a court verdict in Ontario, Canada, by Justice Wildman in Hamdy vs Hamdy, just to cite another example "…gender is, of course, irrelevant in determining spousal support.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As shared during my speech last year during the debate on the Women’s Charter (Amendment) Bill, divorce is one of the most stressful events in one’s life, according to the Holmes and Rahe Stress Scale, second only to the death of a loved one.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This result does not come as a surprise due to the fear of navigating through many uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a result, matters relating to divorce and subsequent related enforcement or variation applications remain as one of the most common topics enquired by applicants for preliminary legal advice at various community legal clinics run across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the course of my legal practice, I have represented clients in matrimonial disputes with a view to resolving matters through what is now commonly known by many as the “Therapeutic Justice” or TJ approach.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many a time, clients and fellow members of the bar have asked, "What exactly is TJ?" To me, in essence, TJ revolves around reducing acrimony in family proceedings, ensuring outcomes are deemed as practical and acceptable to parties involved without undue delays, complexity and unnecessary escalation of costs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, there have been ongoing discussions about transitioning family law proceedings towards such less adversarial TJ approach, just as what the hon Presiding Judge of the Family Justice Courts, Justice Debbie Ong, had shared in the Family Justice Work Plan in 2020.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since then, the Courts and the family practice community have been co-creating a renewed vision of family justice informed by the TJ principles.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, to date, my observation is that the relevant stakeholders still have different interpretations on how a TJ approach ought to be adopted during the Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Moreover, some may still be resistant to buy in to this concept.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In order for this vision to come into fruition, it requires the whole ecosystem to embrace the concept, including the Courts, lawyers, counsellors and the parties involved.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Together, we must work towards a common defined goal that the resolution of family disputes need not be adversarial but should rather be focused on solutions, such as determining what outcome would be the most reasonable and practical in the best interest of the children after their parents have separated.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To achieve this, both the "hardware" and "heartware" changes are necessary.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will ensure that the Courts are adequately equipped to handle cases in a timely and efficient manner.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Moreover, it seems to me that the workload and job scope of MEOs are expected to be heavy, having the need to deal with not just the parties involved but also third parties like the Government agencies and financial institutions to obtain information on parties’ financial situations and, thereafter, conducting conciliation sessions with parties and reporting these developments to the Court.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, the family judges undergo specialist curriculum training in multidisciplinary topics, whereas the family lawyers may opt to attend the Family Therapeutic Justice Certification Programme, and counsellors attend family counselling certification programmes respectively.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Training for all of these relevant family justice community personnel should be carried out together, where all can partake in various role-play scenarios and have a better understanding of one another’s positions by putting themselves in one another’s shoes and explore how they can better work together to resolve those supposed acrimonious issues.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Hopefully, these changes will gradually help to create an environment where parties involved are more inclined to consider and accept the TJ outcomes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of the proposed changes under this Family Justice Reform Bill pertains to enhancing a judge-led approach.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To better promote efficiency in Court proceedings, being another objective which this Reform Bill aims to achieve, I would urge all parties involved, including the judge, lawyers and the parties in action to actively work towards reaching a global settlement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In cases involving children, it should be made mandatory under the Court’s Practice Direction for parties to exchange supporting documents at the outset, which would typically only be exchanged either during the mediation or at the ancillary stage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the matter still cannot be settled and has to proceed under the ordinary route, the docketed judge should promptly refer the matter for mediation, with the aim of converting parties to adopt a TJ mindset and work towards a global settlement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Additionally, MSF or the Court should arrange at the earliest opportunity for the children to undergo counselling to better understand and minimise the trauma caused to the young and innocent as a result of their parents’ divorce.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As Mahatma Gandhi once said, "An eye for an eye only makes the whole world blind." The dissolution of a marriage and parting ways with your spouse need not and should not be acrimonious.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is my sincere hope that this approach can be achieved in all cases, particularly those involving children, once the Bill has been passed and implemented.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Family Justice Reform Bill, when it comes into effect, will give the presiding judge more control.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Deputy Speaker, notwithstanding the clarifications and suggestions I have raised earlier, I stand in support of this Reform Bill.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us all work together towards a future where families can navigate the challenges of separation with dignity, empathy and the welfare of our children at the forefront.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are two parts of this Bill which I wish to speak on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Clause 81 – Court Orders on Maintenance enforcement application.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Currently, when a complainant applies to Court for enforcement of maintenance, the frustration is always with the possible delays in the receipt of the maintenance.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Delays happen when the respondent does not turn up; the case is then adjourned.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The next time the respondent turns up, he applies for adjournment to engage a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, the Court sends parties for mediation and the case is adjourned again while parties try to find an amicable solution.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the respondent disputes the claim, the Court will direct parties to prepare their case and more time is taken up.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the meantime, the complainant suffers because of the time required to attend Court again and again and the failure to receive the maintenance which had been ordered to be paid to the applicant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even if the respondent were to eventually make payment of the arrears of maintenance, there is this possibility that he may default in payment again, then the applicant has to start the process all over again.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, there will be times when an applicant may eventually give up on the maintenance application and decide not to enforce the order.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The MEOs would then be empowered to carry out investigations on the assets of the respondent and then report to the judge.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Without the information given by the MEOs, the applicant who is trying to enforce the maintenance order will have a difficult time trying to check what are the respondent's assets.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In addition, the Court should consider making an order that the respondent's credit cards be cancelled until the arrears of maintenance are settled.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Where an MEO finds that a respondent’s conduct in refusing to pay the maintenance is contumacious, I would submit that the Court ought to punish the respondent for wasting the time of the applicant, the MEO and the Courts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The respondent should not be able to get away with delaying the maintenance payment just to frustrate the applicant; and then he walks away without consequence once he pays up the arrears.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, if he loses his job or, sometimes, if the respondent remarries and has to support another family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In situations like these, I expect that the MEO would recommend a variation of the maintenance order.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The loss of income in this case is or would be self-induced with the intent of denying the applicant the maintenance which she ought to be entitled to.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How would the Court also deal with situations where a respondent refuses to pay child maintenance because he is denied access or visitation rights to the child?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will the Court be able to deal with such situations even though the application before the Court is an enforcement of maintenance application?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Or would the Court require a separate application for enforcement of the access rights?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The current legal position is that the Court in making decisions about the child may appoint a Child Representative to the Court or the Court can appoint a trained or professional assessor to make recommendations on the child’s custody or access orders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The appointed assessor would then prepare a Social Welfare Report, or a Custody Evaluation Report or an Access Evaluation Report.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The judge may also ascertain the wishes of the child by conducting an interview with the child and there has been case laws on the power of the judge to do so.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, may I express some reservations about a judge carrying out interviews of the child because a judge is typically an authority in the law.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He or she is not a trained child counsellor who can discern whether a child has been coached to express certain views or is under duress to say positive things about one parent just by one interview.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although some judges may have some degree of training in handling children, the reality is that a judge spends more time analysing the law and the facts applicable to the case.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, unless a judge spends a much, much longer period of time talking with and interviewing the child, I do have some reservations whether a judge is able to make a better assessment of the wishes of a child by a simple interview, compared to trained social workers who will be spending more time talking and interacting with the child and observing the expressions of the child.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, may I ask the Minister to clarify what is the intent of this amendment as the current case law does allow the process.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is it the position of the Government that they prefer that judges carry out the interviews more regularly, as compared to the judge appointing social workers or Child Representative to take care of the child’s interest?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At the end of the day, what is important is how to ascertain what is in the best interest of the child.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is certainly helpful to have a new unit of Maintenance Enforcement Officers (MEOs) set up and given the power to obtain information about the parties' assets and means from entities, including banks and Government agencies, such as CPF Board and HDB, to ensure that those who refuse to pay are dealt with more decisively.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the MEOs could help distinguish between those who cannot afford to pay maintenance and those who have the financial means but refuse to pay, the officers may face challenges if the parties who could have the ability and capability to derive a better income have, indeed, tried his best to do so and chose not to do so to benefit the applicant.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, the officers would still need to work on the acceptance of medical certification from medical practitioners to determine if the respondent's medical conditions are reasonable to justify lower maintenance payments or exclusion of possible imprisonment order for failure to show proof of payment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the officers require the respondent to seek confirmation from only selected medical officers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the case of a bankrupt respondent, will the award and repayment of maintenance payments be prioritised against other creditors?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the presumption, the onus is then on the respondent to show that there was no intention to siphon the assets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Evidence found by the MEO can be used.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I hope MEO could assist the Court in deciding on the percentage allocation and distribution of the sale proceeds of the existing flat or property to minimise the housing needs challenges faced by both parties after divorce.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the saying goes, "Every family has got its own set of problems and it is very difficult for the judge to preside over family affairs".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The presiding judge in divorce cases will have greater controls, including setting restrictions on the cross-examination process in Court to prevent family relations from further disintegrating.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because both parties would try to reveal each other’s faults, the judge would have the power to issue Court orders to protect the interest of the family as well as the children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, if the judge believes that the cross-examination could bring undue stress upon a vulnerable witness, he can set out restrictions on the cross-examination process.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The judge could also interview the children in person to understand their wishes and issue a judgment that serves the children’s interest.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill will also improve the efficiency of the family justice process.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without the Court’s approval, parties cannot raise unnecessary requests which will frustrate or delay the justice process or affect the children negatively.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For couples considering divorce, I hope that they could mend their differences at the end of the day and there should not be any grievances overnight.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The solution of their dispute still lies in them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that it will not be worse off.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.00 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the enhanced Maintenance Enforcement Process (MEP), which simplifies the enforcement of maintenance orders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share who these prescribed third parties may be?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, can the Minister share what are the contemplated timelines that the MEO will seek from the Court for banks and prescribed third parties?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Family lawyers have shared with me that banks take time to respond to their requests for information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the banks have been consulted on their ability to respond within the contemplated timelines?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that conciliation sessions could be used by a party to delay proceedings, can the Minister share whether there is a limit on the number of conciliation sessions that the MEO can conduct?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what are the consequences for a party if they fail to attend or are clearly not participating in good faith on the conciliation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, MEOs will be empowered to obtain information from parties and to submit a report to the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what training will be provided to the MEOs to make discovery of the relevant documents and assess the parties’ actual financial positions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on what the MEO’s report is supposed to set out and whether it will be provided to both parties?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share whether there will be a standard rubric for MEOs to assess parties’ financial positions in preparing the report?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fifth, the Court may vary the original maintenance orders in the MEP.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Applicants may think twice before applying under the MEP if their application may lead to their original maintenance orders being varied.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if it is only under exceptional circumstances that the Court will vary the original maintenance orders in the MEP?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, can the Minister share what factors a Court should take into account before varying the original maintenance orders in the MEP?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the attachment of earnings Court orders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These Court orders direct a party’s employer to deduct a portion of maintenance from their salary to make direct payment to the other party.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 91H allows the Court to determine what payments to a person are earnings that can be directed for the payment of maintenance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The relevant sections set out obligations relating to the respondent’s employer and employment when an attachment of earnings order is made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether earnings from freelance or gig economy work can be deemed earnings?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If such earnings can be subject to an attachment of earnings order, can the Minister clarify how the obligations relating to traditional employers or employment apply where the respondent is engaged in gig work?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on financial counselling for couples undergoing divorce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the public consultation for the RERF Committee’s recommendations, members of the public asked to build up capabilities in financial counselling to help divorcees better manage their new finances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But counselling works best when it starts earlier, long before divorce applications are even filed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, the RERF Committee said in its 2019 report that sorting out finances early when a marriage has broken down is important to avoid disputes and distress later.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MSF may be able to identify families at high-risk of divorce through the various social service agencies and FSCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how MinLaw and MSF are working together at an upstream stage to help families access financial counselling even before the divorce application is filed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, given that parents with children under 21 years old must undergo the Mandatory Co-Parenting Programme (CPP) before filing for divorce, can Minister of State Sun Xueling share if there are plans to incorporate mandatory financial counselling and planning as part of the CPP?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify where an MEO refers parties for financial assistance after reviewing documents submitted by the parties, will the matter still proceed on to conciliation and hearing?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: That would have made a very effective cut in the Committee of Supply Debate.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: You were under five minutes making all those points.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I do have a few questions and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Family Justice Rules can set out the mode by which the child’s wishes may be determined, including a judicial interview with the child.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, depending on the age and maturity of the child, the child's views can be easily swayed by other family members or persons with vested interest.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Should we set clear safeguards in legislation to allow only children who are mature enough to convey their views independently?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The two are clearly different and it is, therefore, important that we make a distinction between the two.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would the threshold be specified in subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How will the Government ensure that a spouse in an acrimonious divorce case is unable to game the MEP system?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Compared to the current mediation process, MEOs will be accorded powers to actively seek information and recommend practical solutions to the parties involved.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I find this useful, but I do have a few questions on the new MEP.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What kind of training will be provided to MEOs to ensure that they understand and are equipped to apply their new powers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would it be an offence for a person to refuse to comply with an MEO’s direction to seek financial assistance, just to vex the ex-spouse and not provide any maintenance?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, while I welcome the efforts to reform the system to facilitate more sustainable maintenance outcomes, we must also be mindful of indirectly creating the unintended consequence where divorce becomes too easy and becomes the first solution or the quick fix which couples in distress turn to.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must redouble our efforts to strengthen the institution of marriage, so that we have stronger marriages and lower divorce rates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Only by doing so can our children grow up in a strong family nucleus and nurturing family environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I have raised in this House various ideas on various occasions on how we can do so, from improving the quality of our marriage preparation programmes, to having more campaigns to help couples reaffirm their marriages at key milestones.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government will consider my proposals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But even as we facilitate more sustainable maintenance outcomes, we must always remember that prevention is better than cure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us continue to work, as a whole of society, to strengthen marriages and family ties.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although Singapore, as a society, is primarily anchored on family-centric values, with the Government and the community at large encouraging marriages and supportive of couples through their marriages, we acknowledge that some marriages may inevitably break down, due to multifaceted factors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We do need to help couples deal with the fall-out from the break-up of their marriage and help both parties move on with their lives, especially if there are children involved.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I am very supportive of the introduction of the Family Justice Reform Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would like to raise two considerations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, with regard to the new Maintenance Enforcement Process (MEP) and two, on the non-payment of maintenance and how the process could be enhanced to support more applicants, especially the vulnerable ones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Like my concerns shared in my previous speech on the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Bill relating to the process of applying for Lasting Power of Attorney, the process for the enforcement of maintenance assumes that all applicants are tech-savvy and will not have any difficulties applying online.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, we know that there will be cases where applicants are not tech-savvy and may be discouraged to submit an online enforcement application because they are unable to do so readily, even if they are facing financial hardship.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wonder if MSF and MinLaw could work together to identify vulnerable individuals, such as low-income single parents, or divorcees with special needs or disabilities, including those due to stroke, that would require more support in their application and enforcement for maintenance.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A suggestion is for MinLaw and MSF to consider empowering Social Service Office (SSO) or social workers with the role to act on behalf of such applicants, in their navigation of the online application and appropriate referral to the Family Justice Court if they are found to require additional attention to expedite enforcement of their maintenance, especially where the welfare of young children is at stake.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite these safeguards, there may be instances where respondents continue to act irresponsibly and are defiant to these orders, failing to pay maintenance, especially after one year from the hearing.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such instances, I would like to ask what powers and directions the Courts are vested with to ensure that the maintenance order would be fully enforced within a reasonable stipulated time, for the respondents to be brought to task expediently to reduce hardship on the applicants needing the maintenance.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She is a single mother in her early 30s with three young children, aged three to seven.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Meanwhile, Mdm Goh has been relying on ComCare support, which was reduced recently.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While she understands that ComCare assistance is provided only for short to mid-term and she needs to get a job, she has only been able to convince employers to let her work on daily hour-rated jobs because of her need to rush home to care for her young children before and after school or childcare hours, alone.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She also has to wrestle with her bankruptcy status due to her former husband using her name against her will for a loan on which he defaulted.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Her own parents struggle with mental health challenges and are deemed unsuitable for caregiving of her young children by social workers assisting her.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thankful to SSO's help to my appeal, she is given some ComCare extension while I assist her in finding jobs nearer to her home.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given her unresolved maintenance payments from her former husband, which may never be paid, she may be a genuine single parent who will require ComCare assistance to be maintained at a level for a few more years until her two younger children also enter primary school and when she can hopefully find a full-time job with her ITE qualification.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, in recent years, our divorce rate has been on the rise.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, it is extremely important to simplify and strengthen our family justice process.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I strongly support the Family Justice Reform Bill jointly drafted by MinLaw and MSF.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will allow marriages to end in a harmonious manner and safeguard the welfare of the children through a therapeutic justice system.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have two suggestions on the Bill which I hope MinLaw and MSF will consider.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the family justice process set out in the Bill requires divorcees to apply for maintenance online.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am worried that online applications will deter divorcees who are not tech-savvy and will indirectly affect them and their children's welfare.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope MinLaw and MSF will work together to identify vulnerable groups who need help, such as low-income divorcees who are single parents, and provide more social assistance to help them claim maintenance effectively.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that MinLaw and MSF can authorise social workers to apply to the Court for alimony on behalf of the divorcee when necessary, such as when the welfare of the children is seriously affected.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, I would like to relate the story of my resident, Mdm Goh.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, given that most divorces are likely to occur between five and nine years of marriage, the psychological impact towards separation and divorce can be substantial and long-lasting.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is even more so if the couples have young children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, let me conclude my speech by affirming the efforts of MinLaw and MSF in their determination to reform and strengthen Therapeutic Justice elements in the family justice system.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, I also hope that this Bill will help vulnerable individuals, especially those that may have been through an abusive marriage, to regain themselves swiftly and rebuild their lives.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my law practice, I handle some matrimonial cases on a pro bono basis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One such case was when I was assigned by the Legal Aid Bureau to represent a young mother of four in a divorce proceeding.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That case shaped my thinking on how we can and should make it easier for estranged spouses to claim maintenance for their children when divorce occurs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Unfortunately, she was in an abusive relationship, suffering under the hands of an abusive husband she once loved.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She was a housewife with no other sources of income and was wholly dependent on the sole breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She endured the strain of the relationship and the pain of the abuse and held on because of her young children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She would have had a fifth child if not for a miscarriage that she suffered after a beating so bad that she was hospitalised for a week.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The doctors had to perform a hysterectomy and she can never have another child ever again.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, she was faced back then with a system that was cumbersome and daunting for a single mother to navigate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The ex-spouse had sought to kick her and the children out of the matrimonial flat because she was not listed as an owner and refused to agree to any division of assets in her favour.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She finally sought help from the Legal Aid Bureau.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She had to go to the Family Court, as it then was, to seek enforcement and variation of maintenance orders to feed her children and, at the same time, sort out her divorce proceedings before the Syariah Court, a Court case that was protracted by the ex-spouse all the way to the appellate stage.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recalled the maintenance order which, I found, was out of the ordinary.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Typically, such orders would set out the amount to be paid for each child or spouse and the bank account details for such sums to be deposited.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, this one had not only the usual quantum and such details, but it also specified exactly what items that this ex-spouse had to purchase for the children, things like baby formula milk, diapers and even to specify the type of necessities – basic stuff like food and educational expenses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What kind of parent must be told and compelled to purchase sustenance for his own children?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The ex-spouse had not only protracted proceedings but also taken such acrimonious and unreasonable positions which necessitated such specific orders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She told me that she was fortunate to receive legal aid.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is in this spirit that I stand fully in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also welcome the protection of family violence survivors through limited cross-examination in certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As raised in previous Parliamentary speeches, I hope that there can be default video conferencing facilities within the Family Justice Court (FJC) for young survivors to give evidence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is to insulate them from further trauma on the stand.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that such infrastructure is already part of MinLaw's plans and I look forward to the implementation in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have the following further clarifications and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Further, as MEOs encounter members of the public and, to a certain degree, may face hostile respondents or uncooperative third parties, may I ask what are the protection and immunity that will be accorded to MEOs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is to allow would-be public service employers and banks to conduct due diligence for checks on background or credit worthiness.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, on claiming for past outstanding maintenance, one clarification that I have received is whether there is a time limitation period to make such claims under the MEP.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Typically, as in the story I shared earlier, the victim would have had to endure many years of unpaid maintenance through protracted proceedings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, not everyone would make a claim immediately upon breach.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fourthly, in some cases, there are other competing creditors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The usual refrain from the ex-spouse is that he or she had to pay off other loans or financial commitments first.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The financial strain on the paying party is real.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially in cases where the respondent has been declared bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In most cases, the applicant is unlikely to be able to recover any monies from an insolvent respondent.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, in this situation, what are the additional support that can be rendered to both parties?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that the reforms do not change the order of the priorities of an insolvent debtor.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In bankruptcy proceedings, if there had been unfair preference or transactions at undervalue, those assets can be clawed back.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I look forward to understanding how the proposed MEP and the current bankruptcy regime will work together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   This amendment Bill will help applicants, like ex-spouses, to receive any outstanding maintenance much faster and allow the Courts, through its officers and special office, such as the MEO, to obtain the latest information on the financial status and income of relevant parties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will address the points raised in relation to the new Maintenance Enforcement Process (MEP) and the enhancement of Court proceedings and procedures in the FJC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will start with the Members’ questions on the scope of the new MEP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim hopes that the MEP will apply to the enforcement of Syariah Court orders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain also asked about past outstanding maintenance and limitation periods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Bill does not change the existing position on limitation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The applicant will then be able to include those arrears in future enforcement applications if the arrears remain unpaid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the applicant acts in a timely manner, the respondent cannot circumvent his or her obligations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On past maintenance arrears, the MEP will, when fully implemented, apply to all maintenance enforcement applications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai has asked about MEOs being sited under the Executive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The new MEOs will gather evidence and carry out conciliation to help parties reach a sustainable solution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, if parties do not settle, the Court will still make a final decision, possibly using information and evidence gathered by the MEO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is, therefore, preferable for the MEOs’ evidence gathering and conciliation roles to be independent of the Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have discussed this with the Judiciary, which supported the proposal for the MEOs to be sited within the Executive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: AGC’s advice was also sought on the matter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked who we intend to prescribe as the third parties from whom MEOs may seek information.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about information on foreign assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The MEOs and the Singapore Courts do not have powers to direct third parties in a foreign jurisdiction to provide information.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the contemplated timelines to disclose information sought.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have been engaging the banks and third parties that we intend to prescribe and we will work with them to implement the MEP, which would include response timelines.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai also raised the concern that assets may be held in the name of proxies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Pillai also requested for clarification on the ambit of a “third party” under the Bill and whether a third party may be asked to disclose information relating to proxies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The third party may be any person who has relevant information.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thus, if an MEO, in the course of fact-finding, has reason to suspect that the respondent has assets that are held in the name of proxies, the MEO may seek a Court order for a third party to disclose information about the assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is for the Court to decide if such information is relevant to the enforcement application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are limits to the MEOs’ powers to uncover every fact.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is, ultimately, the primary responsibility of the parties to be forthright about their true financial positions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Furnishing false information, when asked by an MEO, or to the Court, is a criminal offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the number of conciliation sessions and the consequences for failing to attend or not participating in good faith.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Bill does not impose a limit on the number of conciliation sessions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We envisage that there will, typically, be two sessions, but the exact number will vary.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is the Court that directs the parties to attend conciliation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Failure to attend is, therefore, contempt of Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Further, if the respondent is absent from conciliation, the Court may direct the respondent to attend another conciliation session.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court may also proceed with the hearing of the application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the respondent is absent for the hearing of the application, the new Family Justice Rules will allow the Court to proceed to make the appropriate orders, if certain conditions are satisfied.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This should also address Ms Ng Ling Ling’s question about her resident whose application got “stuck” because the ex-husband could not be found.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With respect to parties who do not participate in good faith, the parties’ conduct during conciliation will be set out in the MEO’s report to the Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court may take the parties’ conduct into account in making the appropriate orders on the maintenance enforcement application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the matter will still proceed to hearing after the MEO refers parties for financial assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Financial assistance is not intended to replace the parties’ financial responsibilities to their families, but acts as a safety net for our fellow Singaporeans in need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The matter will, therefore, still proceed for conciliation and hearing after the MEO makes the referral for financial assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The MEO will take into account the financial assistance granted, if any, as part of the overall assessment of the financial circumstances of the parties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court will also take into consideration information on any financial assistance granted, in deciding on the appropriate orders to be made.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about whether it is an offence for a respondent to refuse financial assistance, despite an MEO's referral.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is open to a respondent to decide whether to accept financial assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will turn to Mr Louis Ng and Mr Dennis Tan's queries on what the MEO’s report will set out and whether the reports will be provided to both parties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It will contain all the information submitted to the MEO in relation to the maintenance enforcement application; matters relating to the conciliation sessions; and any other matters and information as may be prescribed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In respect of interim reports, the clause which Mr Dennis Tan referred to allows the MEO to provide an interim report to the applicant only, first, to cater for a situation where the MEO needs to inform the applicant of an impending dissipation of assets so that appropriate action can be taken.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The intent is for the interim report to eventually be available to both parties in accordance with the rules.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The intention is for the MEO to provide all relevant facts and evidence for the Court’s consideration.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court may then, if it thinks fit, rely on the MEO’s report to make the appropriate orders against the respondent’s assets, without calling for further evidence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We may prescribe additional matters to be covered in the report, as we learn from the initial phases of implementation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Dennis Tan has also asked what information may be redacted from the MEO's report.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The MEO has broad powers to gather information for the Court from third parties, including information that is ordinarily private and confidential.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There may be information gathered by the MEO and in the report that is unnecessary or irrelevant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This power will allow for such information to be redacted to protect the party's interests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Melvin Yong also asked whether there is a standard rubric for MEOs to assess the parties’ financial position.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh referred to challenges with distinguishing between those who will not pay and cannot pay cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Each case will be assessed on its facts, based on information on the parties’ assets and means.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: That being said, the MEOs will be trained and given guidelines on making these assessments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will work closely with Social Service Officers from MSF to develop these guidelines.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ultimately, it is for the Court to decide whether the respondent cannot pay or refuses to pay, and the appropriate orders to make.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court will consider the MEO’s report in coming to its decision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The FJC judges are trained to deal with a wide range of family situations and also have the powers to make orders to address the unique needs of each family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They will also be supported by counsellors and other professionals who will be able to provide therapeutic interventions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, if a respondent is retrenched and has challenges paying maintenance due to the sudden loss of income, the Court may suspend the maintenance order or vary the maintenance amount downwards for a short period of time and make the appropriate directions for the respondent to report back to the Court on a specified date after he or she has had time to look for a new job.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court may also make an order requiring the respondent to undergo financial counselling with a professional counsellor who will be able to help the respondent explore various options to manage his or her daily expenses and to pay maintenance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also suggested that the MEOs may also assist the Court at the stage of division of matrimonial assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We thank Mr Gan for his suggestion, which we will study.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Melvin Yong, Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Hany Soh have asked about MEOs’ recruitment, training and resourcing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These are operational details that will be worked through in implementation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Suffice to say that we intend to hire and train a multidisciplinary team, with team members having or being trained and equipped with knowledge and skills in different areas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will include the skills needed to effectively manage the parties in family proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also thank Ms Hany Soh for her suggestion on taking a coordinated approach across the entire family justice ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will certainly keep this in mind as we develop the training programmes in a way that strengthens therapeutic justice outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain has asked about legal protections for the MEOs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Bill gives the MEOs protection against personal liability when they exercise their powers or perform their functions or duties, provided they do so in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will now address the questions and comments that Members have raised with respect to the powers of the Court hearing the maintenance enforcement application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, on the Court's powers to vary the maintenance orders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Louis Ng expressed concern that the potential for variation may disincentivise some applicants from applying for enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also asked about variation where the respondent loses his or her job or if he or she has a new family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: What the MEP does is to reduce the procedural challenges that parties face in seeking variation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court will consider all relevant facts and circumstances before deciding whether there has been any change in circumstances warranting a variation of the maintenance order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: New financial commitments and loss of job could be relevant considerations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, the Courts have held that remarriage per se does not affect pre-existing obligations owed to the family from an earlier marriage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Similarly, when MEOs make recommendations to parties to facilitate an out-of-Court settlement, remarriage and loss of job are but two of the various factors that will be considered.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Maintenance orders would not be varied in cases where the respondent has the means to pay the maintenance sum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In cases where the respondent has genuinely experienced a change in circumstances affecting his or her ability to pay maintenance, the MEP will help the Court make a more accurate assessment of the nature of the change and accordingly make more accurate variation orders where needed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This can be a temporary variation to deal with a temporary change in circumstances, but it leads to a more sustainable outcome for all parties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On the other hand, if we turn a blind eye to the changed circumstances, respondents will continue to miss maintenance payments time and time again, even if multiple enforcement applications are made and concluded against them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Applicants will spend time and costs on enforcement, only to end up being disappointed each time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It would be far better for such applicants to receive the appropriate financial assistance and other forms of support, or enter into a more sustainable maintenance arrangement with the respondent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also asked about the circumstances in which a respondent would not be imprisoned, or lower maintenance amounts ordered, because of his or her medical conditions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These are decisions that are, ultimately, for the Court to make, taking into account all the circumstances of the case.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Where there are disputes of fact, for example, on the medical conditions of the respondent, the MEO may help to gather the relevant facts and evidence, including seeking information from third parties to verify the parties' positions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court may also direct the MEOs to conduct further fact-finding, if necessary.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Attachment of earnings orders work effectively where there is a regular and stable stream of income that can be directed towards the fulfilment of periodical maintenance payments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They do not work so well where the income is unpredictable, such as for freelancers and contract workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Where incomes are not stable, the family's financial situation is naturally more complicated and it is not always easy to find simple solutions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The MEOs will help parties look at the overall picture and suggest arrangements that are sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ultimately, regardless of the type of work one does, the respondent must be responsible for fulfilling his or her obligations for maintenance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Even if the attachment of earnings order is not available, there are various other ways to hold them accountable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Dennis Tan said that respondents who delay paying maintenance to frustrate the complainant should not be allowed to walk away without consequences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Bill allows for consequences to be imposed on such respondents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, the Court may imprison a respondent who has no good reason for failing to pay maintenance on time, even if that respondent pays up after the applicant files the enforcement application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Further, for a respondent who has not paid maintenance in a timely manner and the parties have not settled, the Court must make a Show-Payment Order for the Respondent to show proof of payment of any future maintenance payable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: An imprisonment term may also be specified for the breach of the Show-Payment Order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Lim also asked about situations where the respondent refuses to pay because he or she is denied access to the child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Being denied access is not grounds for non-compliance with a maintenance order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A parent has a legal duty to maintain a child, whether the child is in his or her custody or not.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the respondent is denied access to the child, he or she may take up an application for the enforcement of the access order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will now address some of the other comments made or questions asked in relation to maintenance enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain suggested that all maintenance orders be placed on a searchable database registry and that a recalcitrant defaulter can be placed on a blacklist with an alert to the Credit Service Bureau.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Women's Charter already provides for an Applicant who has filed for maintenance enforcement to be able to lodge a report to a designated credit bureau regarding unpaid arrears stated on the order of Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Applicants will continue to be able to lodge such reports under the new MEP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Under the new MEP, the MEO may also assist to lodge the arrears report.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This may be helpful for applicants who have challenges filing the arrears report on their own.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Gan has also asked whether maintenance payments will be prioritised over other debts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain has asked for clarification on how the new MEP and the bankruptcy regime will interface with each other.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As Mr Zhulkarnain has correctly mentioned, the reforms in this Bill do not change the order of priorities of an insolvent debtor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The reforms also do not change how enforcement proceedings or orders ordinarily interact with the bankruptcy regime.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr Gan have also asked what can be done when respondents are declared bankrupt or respondents are struggling financially.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Dr Wan Rizal raised concerns of harshness on parties genuinely unable to pay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain mentioned that for bankrupt respondents, applicants are unlikely to be able to recover any arrears but yet are saddled with the expenses of the children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is where the reforms under the MEP may be helpful.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This would include considering, like what Mr Gan said, whether the respondent has genuine responsibilities paying for their children and elderly parents' expenses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and Mr Zhulkarnain asked if there can be more practical help for vulnerable individuals and laypersons applying to enforce their maintenance orders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The new process was designed specifically to reduce the burden on parties, especially Self-represented Persons (SRPs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Nonetheless, certain litigants may still require more help than others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, there are various physical touchpoints where such SRPs can seek help in filing a maintenance enforcement application, such as: the ServiceSG Centres at Our Tampines Hub and One Punggol, the Divorce Support Specialist Centres (DSSAs) and the Singapore Council of Women's Organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will work with ServiceSG and MSF to ensure that such services continue to be offered even after the new Maintenance Enforcement Process is implemented.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will work together with our partners and stakeholders in the legal and social service sectors to disseminate information on and raise awareness of the MEP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain reiterated his support for empowering judges to impose restrictions on cross-examination in prescribed circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: He also mentioned video conferencing facilities for young survivors to give evidence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As Mr Zhulkarnain noted – and he would be glad to know – video conferencing facilities for victims of family violence are already available at the FJC today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Family Court may permit the giving of evidence through a live video or live television link, in family violence proceedings under the Women's Charter, where certain conditions are satisfied, including where the witness is below the age of 18.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court will assess the relevant facts and circumstances of each case to decide if such permission should be given.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
